checkpoints: Put one NGINX Ingress Controller behind the single cloud LoadBalancer and let it fan out by host, instead of exposing `api-service` and `web-service` on their own.

The routing contract is two host rules on one Ingress object: `api.example.com` with `pathType: Prefix` on `/` forwards to `api-service:PORT`, and `app.example.com` with the same path shape forwards to `web-service:PORT`.
TLS termination lives at that same Ingress — a `spec.tls` block per host, each naming its own secret.
cert-manager watches the Ingress's `cluster-issuer` annotation to request and write the Let's Encrypt certificate into each secret automatically.
The NGINX controller loads those secrets to terminate HTTPS right at the edge, so neither backend Pod ever has to handle a certificate itself.

Defend the "just spin up a second LoadBalancer" objection directly: a cloud LoadBalancer usually carries its own separate monthly charge and its own public IP, so fanning many Services out through one Ingress is the cost- and IP-efficient path.
It also means `api-service` and `web-service` stay ClusterIP-only, never directly reachable from the Internet — the Ingress is the one public door.

It scales cleanly: onboarding a third service later is one more host rule and one more `tls` entry on the exact same Ingress object, no new LoadBalancer or cert-manager wiring needed, and cert-manager keeps renewing every host's cert on its own well before expiry.
The first extraction step turns on a gateway sitting in front: most paths still route to the monolith exactly as they do now.

Exactly ONE path (say `/api/payment`) is redirected to a newly extracted payment-service, running side by side with the monolith until it fully "shrinks away" — that's the core idea of the strangler fig, not a big-bang rewrite.

Choosing Payment first has to rest on a real signal: if load between the two modules is clearly skewed — Payment spikes many times over during a sale while Search barely moves — extracting Payment lets you scale exactly the bottleneck instead of replicating the whole block.
If the team owning Payment is already clearly separate from the team owning Search (Conway's Law), that's also a valid boundary signal.

The extraction boundary has to sit along a real bounded context — Payment is already a distinct module in code, not cut mid-way through a business flow — otherwise you end up with a distributed monolith (services split physically but still calling each other chatty, forced to deploy together).

The migration's safety comes from keeping the gateway's contract stable: the client still calls `/api/payment` exactly as before, with no idea the route now points somewhere new — this is what lets you extract one capability at a time, the monolith shrinking gradually instead of a full rewrite.
The data boundary: the new payment-service owns its own data, so any operation still needing both Search and Payment in one flow no longer fits inside a single DB's ACID transaction.
It has to move to eventual consistency, using a Saga/outbox pattern with a compensating action to "undo" when a step fails partway through, instead of an atomic rollback.
Pod IPs are ephemeral — every Pod recreation (an OOM restart, a drained node, or even an ordinary rolling update) gets a completely new IP.
Hardcoding an IP into MYSQL_HOST guarantees the config breaks on the very next MySQL recreate, not some rare edge case.
The correct fix is pointing the backend at the Service's stable DNS name, MYSQL_HOST=mysql-service.
CoreDNS resolves that name to mysql-service's ClusterIP.
The Service determines membership through selector: app=mysql — it isn't pinned to one specific Pod.

The Service keeps tracking and updating its Endpoints list to whichever Pods currently carry that label and are healthy, which is what keeps the address stable while the Pod behind it dies and comes back with a new IP.
This is service discovery: Kubernetes hides Pod-IP ephemerality behind a name that never moves.
The result: the backend's config never has to change whenever a MySQL Pod gets replaced — point it at the Service name once, and Kubernetes handles the moving-IP part behind the scenes from then on.
"More modern" is not a reason — it names a trend, not a trade-off.
The real trade-off is that splitting turns an in-process function call into a network call that must handle retries and eventual consistency.
None of the actual split signals are present: 4 engineers is not enough to divide service ownership across separate teams.
There's no evidence yet of one module's load outpacing the others.
Worse, the bounded context itself is still unstable, with the team actively reshuffling how Accounts, Catalog, and Checkout should even be divided.
Splitting now means redrawing that boundary over and over again across the network instead of inside one codebase.

The likely result is a distributed monolith: three services still tightly coupled and forced to deploy together, paying the full operational cost of microservices while getting none of the independent-scaling or fault-isolation benefit.

The recommendation is to stay a monolith — or a modular monolith with clean in-code module boundaries — and revisit the split later with strangler fig once a module genuinely needs independent scale or a team is large enough to own it outright.
Liveness answers "is this Pod still alive, or must I restart it"; readiness answers a completely different question — "is this Pod ready to receive traffic".
Only Pods that readiness reports as "ready" get added to the Service's Endpoints; a Pod that isn't ready simply never receives requests from the Service.

Without a readinessProbe, Kubernetes has nothing to go on but the Pod's "Running" status to decide whether to add it to Endpoints — "Running" only means the container has started, not that the app has finished connecting to MySQL/Redis.

The result: in exactly those few seconds while the app is still connecting to the DB, the new Pod is already pushed into Endpoints and starts receiving real traffic, so those requests land on a not-ready Pod and return transient 5xx errors.

This is precisely why the rolling update loses its zero-downtime guarantee: it relies on readiness to know when a new Pod is safe to receive traffic without dropping requests, and without that signal Kubernetes can't distinguish "Running" from "actually ready" so it shifts traffic early anyway.

The inverse is worth noting too: if the livenessProbe is configured too aggressively (short timeout, low threshold), it can restart Pods that are merely slow — say, working through a heavy query — rather than actually hung, causing needless disruption even though the system is perfectly healthy.
A distributed monolith is a set of services that have been physically split but still behave like one block: they call each other synchronously, chattily, and are forced to deploy together.

This means paying the full network and operational cost of microservices (tracing, service discovery, retries, timeouts) without getting back the independent deploy/scale/fault-isolation benefit that was the whole reason to split in the first place.

The clearest tell-tale sign: changing one service always forces you to change and redeploy one or more other services too — this shows up because the service boundaries were drawn along the existing code structure rather than the domain's real bounded contexts.

This is exactly why a bad split can be worse than no split: fixing a wrong boundary over the network is far more expensive than fixing it inside one codebase, because every redraw means a contract change, release coordination across multiple teams, and the risk of a breaking change rippling into another service.

On top of that, crossing a service boundary already trades away single-DB ACID: an order-plus-debit operation that used to fit inside one transaction now spans multiple services, so it has to move to eventual consistency.
That eventual consistency is handled using Saga or the outbox pattern with compensating actions to "undo" a partway failure, instead of one atomic rollback.

Bottom line: don't split before the domain has stabilized or before you have real signals (a team big enough to divide ownership, clearly skewed load across modules) — keep a modular monolith so the boundaries stay in code, cheap to redraw, and only extract via strangler fig once those signals are actually there.
port-forward can never prove or disprove round-robin: it opens a direct tunnel straight to one target Pod, bypassing kube-proxy and the Service's routing entirely.
So every call through port-forward always lands on that same Pod regardless of how many replicas exist or how well load balancing is actually working.
To actually observe balancing, you have to call the Service's ClusterIP DNS name from inside the cluster — that path goes through kube-proxy.
kube-proxy reads the Endpoints list (the healthy Pods matching the Service's selector) and installs routing rules (iptables or IPVS) on the node that spread requests round-robin across those Pods.
That mechanism has a hard ceiling: kube-proxy operates at L4 — it round-robins connections/packets with no notion of load, so it cannot tell one Pod is CPU-pinned while another sits idle.
It also has no notion of HTTP — it cannot read a path like /checkout or a header to route differently.
The moment you need load-aware balancing or L7 routing decisions (path-based, host-based, header-based canary), kube-proxy's L4 round-robin is the wrong tool for the job.
That's exactly when you put an Ingress controller or a service mesh sidecar in front of the Service to add that L7 intelligence.
A Service binds to Pods purely by label, never by name.
The selector here was typo'd to `app: status-service-typo`, which no Pod carries.
Because no Pod matches, `kubectl get endpoints status-service` comes back `<none>`.
Every request black-holes — hangs then times out, no HTTP error at all — because the ClusterIP still exists validly and nothing actively rejects the packet.
The fix is to set the selector back to `app: status-service`, and it must match `template.metadata.labels` on the Deployment exactly.
Verify with `kubectl get endpoints status-service` showing real Pod IPs, then re-curl to confirm traffic recovers.
Lesson: `kubectl get endpoints` is always the first debugging step whenever traffic can't reach a Pod.

The cause isn't in the app's code but in the probe configuration itself: `livenessProbe` starts calling `/health` after only `initialDelaySeconds: 2`, while the app needs about 30 seconds to connect to MySQL and run first-boot DDL before `/health` returns `200`.
At second 2, the app hasn't finished connecting yet, so `/health` isn't ready (timeout or error), which makes the probe fail.
Once `failureThreshold` consecutive failures are hit, the kubelet considers the container 'dead' and kills it, restarting it under the default policy.
`initialDelaySeconds` resets to zero for the new startup, so the container never gets a full 30 uninterrupted seconds to finish booting before being killed again, producing an infinite restart loop.
Fix: raise `initialDelaySeconds` to cover the real startup time (e.g. 30 seconds or more) and/or raise `failureThreshold`.
A more robust approach when boot time can vary is to add a dedicated `startupProbe` that holds liveness off until `startupProbe` reports success once, after which liveness starts probing normally.
`readinessProbe` (not liveness) is the correct mechanism to keep the Pod out of the Service pool while it's still booting, with no container restart needed at all.
Verify: `kubectl get pods -w` shows the Pod reach `1/1 Running` with `RESTARTS: 0` and stay stable over time, and `/health` returns `200` right once MySQL is connected.
`postgres.image.tag` is the wrong key path — the chart uses `postgresql.*` — so Helm silently ignores the mistyped override and keeps the old default image.
'helm install succeeded' proves nothing about whether the override actually took effect.
Required before merge: run `helm template -f values.yaml` and grep the rendered `image:` line to confirm the override actually landed.
The hardcoded production password in `values.yaml` is a blocker on its own.
A committed secret lives forever in git history, is hard to rotate, and easily leaks into CI/logs.
Fix: inject the credential via `--set-string ...=$ENV`, an `existingSecret`, or external secrets (Vault/Sealed Secrets).
Merge gate: approve only once both hold — the render is verified to carry the right key, and the credential has been taken out of the repo.
